e-9829.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
e-9829.problem:
For the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/d19df62851eeb549464dd522cabcb4f5ab982ed4cdf39a81e6c18642299270f2.png) find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
e-9829.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m \times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n \times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,{4}^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-9828.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
e-9828.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/1727ec75ec656a46caa6228d4b4704643039a194cc2c33419ec8049f63a96a9c.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
e-9828.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$ 

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/877912dffd62a0657f08fc4bc28158e1199daadbda3d92610a0c0f63055f5960.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-9830.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
e-9830.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/95ef5c6139d13a561125764fc1658d03748004b4ee28843a7a3eb8dc7a37504a.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
e-9830.worked_solution:
If $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r ^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V_r \, \Sigma_r^+ \, U_r^T,
$$

where $\Sigma_r^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma_r.$

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/b9efcf7d8dfaa697ebbed69113611e3e669b8c7da27813a9262a7e4e5542dbeb.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}12 & 16 & 0 \\ 9 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

history.worked_solution:

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}

{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

For the matrix A=[3000], find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
13[0001]
b
13[000−1]
c
13[1000]
d
13[−1000]
e
13[100−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[3000]+=[3−1000]=13[1000].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares option c: reciprocate the nonzero diagonal entry 3 and leave the zero unchanged. This agrees with the independent calculation A⁺ = diag(1/3, 0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The pseudoinverse is a 2×3 matrix with nonzero diagonal entries 1/6 and -1/9. Factoring out 1/18 gives diagonal entries 3 and -2, matching option e.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,(-9)^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

For the matrix A=[600−900], find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
19[300020]
b
−19[300020]
c
16[−300020]
d
118[2000−30]
e
118[3000−20]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[600−900]+=[6−1000(−9)−10]=118[3000−20].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,(-9)^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

For the matrix A=[800040], find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
18[201100]
b
14[100200]
c
18[100200]
d
12[200400]
e
18[200100]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[800040]+=[8−1004−100]=18[100200].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares option c, agreeing with the calculation: the 3×2 pseudoinverse has diagonal entries 1/8 and 1/4, with all other entries zero.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[600020]+=[6−1002−100]=16[100300].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
content.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=110[1−331],Σ+=125[1000],UT=12[11−11].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ, the sole nonzero singular value contributes (1/5)([1,2]ᵀ/√5)([1,2]/√5) = (1/25)[[1,2],[2,4]], matching option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=15[1−221],Σ+=15[1000],UT=15[12−21].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=15[1−221]⋅15[1000]⋅15[12−21]=125[1−221]⋅[1000]⋅[12−21]=125[1020]⋅[12−21]=125[1224].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution gives A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ = (1/25)[[1,2],[2,4]], exactly option a. This agrees with the independent calculation.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ, the nonzero singular value contributes (1/2)([1,1]ᵀ/√2)([1,-1,0]/√2) = (1/4)[[1,-1,0],[1,-1,0]], matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

U=[12012−12012010],Σ=[200000],V=[12−121212] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
14[1−11−100]
b
18[1101−10]
c
18[111−100]
d
12[−1101−10]
e
14[1−101−10]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=12[1−111],Σ+=12[100000],UT=12[1−10002110].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=12[1−111]⋅12[100000]⋅12[1−10002110]=14[1−111]⋅[100000]⋅[1−10002110]=14[100100]⋅[1−10002110]=14[1−101−10].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=110[1−331],Σ+=152[100000],UT=15[120005−210].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=110[1−331]⋅152[100000]⋅15[120005−210]=150[1−331]⋅[100000]⋅[120005210]=150[100300]⋅[120005−210]=150[120360].

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares option d, agreeing with A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ = (1/50)[[1,2,0],[3,6,0]]. Its intermediate sign typo in an unused row does not affect the result.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

U=[12−121212],Σ=[210000],V=[25−151525] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=15[2−112],Σ+=1210[1000],UT=12[11−11].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=15[2−112]⋅1210[1000]⋅12[11−11]=120[2−112]⋅[1000]⋅[11−11]=120[2010]⋅[11−11]=120[2211].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}15 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & -5 \\ 10 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=15[21−12],Σr+=130[2003],UrT=15[10−2201].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=15[21−12]⋅130[2003]⋅15[10−2201]=1150[21−12]⋅[2003]⋅[10−2201]=1150[43−26]⋅[10−2201]=1150[100−510010]=130[20−1202].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares A⁺ = (1/30)[[2,0,-1],[2,0,2]], exactly option c. Independent multiplication of VᵣΣᵣ⁻¹Uᵣᵀ confirms this result.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}15 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{150}[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & -5 \\ 10 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{30}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=12[1−111],Σr+=124[4006],UrT=132[−14−1−303].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=12[1−111]⋅124[4006]⋅132[−14−1−303]=1144[1−111]⋅[4006]⋅[−14−1−303]=1144[4−646]⋅[−14−1−303]=1144[1416−22−221614]=172[78−11−1187].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Ur=[12012],Σr=[2],Vr=[12−12] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
14[11−111−1]
b
14[101−10−1]
c
12[10−110−1]
d
12[101101]
e
18[111−11−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=12[1−1],Σr+=12[1],UrT=12[101].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=12[1−1]⋅12[1]⋅12[101]=14[1−1]⋅[1]⋅[101]=14[1−1]⋅[101]=14[101−10−1].

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution declares A⁺ = (1/4)[[1,0,1],[-1,0,-1]], exactly option b. This agrees with independently computing VᵣΣᵣ⁻¹Uᵣᵀ.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Ur=[12−12],Σr=[10],Vr=[1525] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
110[1−22−1]
b
110[2−11−2]
c
110[1−12−2]
d
110[−11−22]
e
110[11−2−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=15[12],Σr+=110[1],UrT=12[1−1].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=15[12]⋅110[1]⋅12[1−1]=110[12]⋅[1]⋅[1−1]=110[12]⋅[1−1]=110[1−12−2].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
after.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=113[32],Σr+=126[1],UrT=12[101].

A+=VrΣr+UrT=113[32]⋅126[1]⋅12[101]=126[32]⋅[1]⋅[101]=126[32]⋅[101]=126[303202].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
content.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
